1.pericope_label: How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger, and cast down from heaven unto the earth the beauty of Israel, and remembered not his footstool in the day of his anger! The Lord hath swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob, and hath not pitied: he hath thrown down in his wrath the strong holds of the daughter of Judah; he hath brought them down to the ground: he hath polluted the kingdom and the princes thereof. He hath cut off in his fierce anger all the horn of Israel: he hath drawn back his right hand from before the enemy, and he burned against Jacob like a flaming fire, which devoureth round about.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch weigh the vocabulary: the verb for swallowing carries the idea of utter annihilation, matching a word for wrath which properly means an overflowing, and the clause about not sparing works adverbially on what precedes. With Ellicott they take the habitations for shepherds' resting-places, hence the open unwalled villages set over against the fortresses named beside them. They also refuse to read these verses as a chronicle of events in their natural order, since that can be managed only by forcing the figures, making every horn stand for the frontier fortresses and the like; the three members form a climax rather than a sequence. Ellicott reads the whole as a thunder-cloud breaking into a tempest, takes the beauty of Israel for the Temple while allowing it might be the heroes who defended it, identifies the footstool as the ark, insists the divine name here is Adonai rather than Jehovah, notes that the word for polluting the kingdom implies it had been a consecrated thing, and makes the horn strength itself, standing for warriors, rulers and fortresses, while improving the last clause to say that God kindled a burning, as one applying a torch.

Gill clears away the wrong senses of the cloud: not a covering of their persons for protection as at the sea and in the wilderness, nor of their sins, which God blots out as a thick cloud, nor the cloud that filled the sanctuary, but the black cloud of calamity, one translator's word for it being that God beclouded her; he also reports a Jewish commentator who read it the other way, that God lifted her to the clouds in order to throw her down harder. Calvin hears the opening as wonder at a prodigy, since a people taken into favour and bound by a perpetual covenant now appeared forsaken, though God does not change with men's perfidy and the promise never rested on merit; he is careful that this is not doubt of God's constancy but a device to soften a nation grown hard under its evils, since nobody calls on God in earnest until humbled. He knows the raising-up reading and supplies its picture, the potter lifting the vessel before dashing it, but judges it too refined; and he ties the profaning of the kingdom back to the forgotten footstool, the kingdom having been consecrated too, so that God in a manner exposed his own name to the mouths of the ungodly.

Clarke sees a veiling rather than a beclouding, the women of the east wearing costly veils and this one a dark cloud; he takes the beauty for the Temple and the footstool for the ark, but records against the usual text that twenty-four of the manuscripts collated by one scholar read Jehovah where the printed text has Adonai. He explains the horn as a figure from cattle, whose strength lies there, and the drawn-back right hand as God's withholding support when the enemy came. He also quotes his old English Bible, which calls the ark his little stepping-stool in the day of his woodness, and explains that to be wood once meant to be mad. Wesley makes the footstool the Temple itself rather than the ark, takes the casting down for a fall from the highest glory to the meanest servitude, and keeps to the fire, which consumed not in this part or that but round about, as flames take a house on every side at once.

Henry finds the weight of the dirge in one place, that the emphasis is not on what was done but on whose hand did it: the grief is not so much that these things happened as that God did them, and that is the wormwood and the gall, since to those who know how to value his favour nothing is more dreadful than his anger, corrections in love being easily borne while rebukes in love wound deeply. He sets the cloud against the pillar in the wilderness, the side now turned toward them being the side that was turned toward the Egyptians, and has the right hand turned back so that they could neither follow a blow nor ward one off.

debates.question: What does the covering with a cloud mean?

positions.position: A beclouding with calamity, darkness drawn over her brightness; the alternative that God raised her up in order to cast her down harder is reported but not adopted.
A veiling, as eastern women are veiled, the veil being a dark cloud.
A thunder-cloud breaking into a tempest.
An enveloping, set against the pillar of cloud that once led them, now turned toward them as it was toward the Egyptians.

debates.question: What is the footstool that was not remembered?

positions.position: The ark of the covenant, which perished with the Temple.
The Temple itself.
The sanctuary God had chosen for himself, whose ruin measures how far his wrath was kindled.

outliers.claim: Quotes his old English Bible, which renders the footstool as his little stepping-stool in the day of his woodness, and explains that to be wood once meant, in that language, to be mad.

Refuses to treat the verses as a chronicle of the siege in natural order, holding that such a reading survives only by forcing the figures, and that the three clauses are a climax rather than a sequence of events.

themes: How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger, and cast down from heaven unto the earth the beauty of Israel, and remembered not his footstool in the day of his anger!

The Lord hath swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob, and hath not pitied: he hath thrown down in his wrath the strong holds of the daughter of Judah; he hath brought them down to the ground: he hath polluted the kingdom and the princes thereof.
He hath cut off in his fierce anger all the horn of Israel: he hath drawn back his right hand from before the enemy, and he burned against Jacob like a flaming fire, which devoureth round about.

4.pericope_label: He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion: he poured out his fury like fire. The Lord was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation. And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle, as if it were of a garden: he hath destroyed his places of the assembly: the Lord hath caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and hath despised in the indignation of his anger the king and the priest. The Lord hath cast off his altar, he hath abhorred his sanctuary, he hath given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they have made a noise in the house of the Lord, as in the day of a solemn feast.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch report and reject an expositor's suggestion that the poet hesitated to say outright that the Lord had become an enemy and broke off his sentence unfinished, ruling it out from the accents, which do not separate the words. On the garden comparison they hold the noun means what is hedged in, therefore the Temple itself, and refuse the usual point of comparison outright: it is not the ease with which a garden or its fence comes down, and the perplexity of expositors here has bred artificial and untenable explanations. Ellicott corrects the verb to destroyed rather than slew, taking in everything dear and not only warriors and youths; identifies the tabernacle of that verse as the city rather than the Temple, the people being collectively the daughter of Zion; notes a change of gender between her palaces and his strongholds, guessing the palaces went with the daughter of Zion and the strongholds with the land, and that the words for mourning and lamentation share a root and chime together; makes the tabernacle of the later verse a booth of the kind raised at the feast, removed as a man removes a shed from an orchard; observes that the word for places of assembly is the same as that for solemn feasts, so the ruin carried feasts and sabbaths with it, king and priest being alike rejected; and hears in the noise of the enemies their triumph, perhaps even their own worship, standing where the festival songs had stood.

Gill notes that such a bow was bent with the foot, and holds God only appears an enemy through the dispensations of providence, as one afflicted man took him to be; he reports a translator who renders the phrase that the Lord is become a very enemy, taking the particle for reality rather than similitude, though he keeps to appearance himself; and he has the sanctuary pulled down as easily as a tent and no more accounted of than a lodge set up in a vineyard at the gathering. Calvin makes the bow a part standing for the whole, so that God was fully armed, and by the right hand understands the enemies themselves, God having held up a banner to them and gone before with an armed hand; he denies the repetition superfluous, since the people were so stupefied by their evils that they never turned their eyes toward God and had to be told at length, lest they take the Chaldeans for the movers of the war rather than men endued with a power not their own. He objects that cottage extenuates the garden comparison too much and takes the verb for removing: God removed his tabernacle as though it were one of the little cottages watchmen keep among the vines, hiding in small chests only until the vintage is in. He measures the whole by saying that for God to cast away altar, sanctuary, ark and festival, the very things by which his favour was sought, was as if heaven and earth had been blended together.

Clarke stages the archer, who bends the bow, sets the arrow on the string, lays his right hand on its lower end and takes aim; passes on a rendering that turns the garden comparison round, making it the garden of his own hedging; says the ordinances were not suspended but destroyed; and observes that where the silver trumpets had sounded there was nothing now but warlike instruments. Wesley identifies the king and priest as the last king and the high priest, one miserably handled and the other killed, glosses the places of assembly as the synagogues, and agrees that the enemies made as great a noise as those who once sang to the glory of God.

debates.question: Is the comparison to an enemy a likeness or a fact?

positions.position: Only an appearance, God seeming an enemy through the dispensations of providence; though a translator is reported who takes the particle for reality rather than similitude.
The words stand as written and the accents forbid the suggestion that the poet flinched from saying it and broke off.
God himself, not the Chaldeans, moved the war, and the point had to be pressed at length because the people would not see it.

debates.question: What is the point of comparing the tabernacle to a garden?

positions.position: Its slightness: pulled down as easily as a tent, and no more regarded than a lodge in a vineyard at harvest.
A booth of the kind raised at the feast, removed as a man removes a temporary shed from an orchard.
Not ease of destruction at all; the noun means what is hedged in, that is the Temple, and the usual comparison has bred artificial explanations.
Not a cottage, which extenuates too much; the verb is to remove, and the figure is the watchman's hut kept among vines only until the vintage.

outliers.claim: Passes on a rendering that inverts the figure entirely, making the phrase mean the garden of God's own hedging rather than a booth taken out of a garden.
Notices that the palaces are feminine and the strongholds masculine in the same verse, and guesses the poet thought of the palaces with the daughter of Zion and the strongholds with the land.

themes: He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion: he poured out his fury like fire.
The Lord was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.

And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle, as if it were of a garden: he hath destroyed his places of the assembly: the Lord hath caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and hath despised in the indignation of his anger the king and the priest.

The Lord hath cast off his altar, he hath abhorred his sanctuary, he hath given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they have made a noise in the house of the Lord, as in the day of a solemn feast.

8.pericope_label: The Lord hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together. Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the Lord. The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, and keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the stretched-out line the systematic thoroughness of the work of destruction, and alone lingers on the mourning rampart, where the very stones of Zion's walls are imagined crying out over their own downfall. On the gates he agrees they are buried under rubbish and adds that they cannot be shut in any case, the bars being gone. He says the law was practically repealed, the conditions of its observance being gone, and prophecy had become a thing of the past, the outward desolation being only the shadow of the spiritual; and he finds the elders' posture a reproach, since instead of taking counsel for the emergency they sit as though the evil were inevitable. Keil and Delitzsch have the silence come from the depth of the sorrow, with the young women renouncing their gaiety and bowing their heads to the ground.

Gill records the older disagreement about which wall is meant, the city's or the one enclosing the Temple and its courts; has the gates broken, levelled and buried under rubbish, and dismisses as a mere fable the rabbinic gloss that they sank into the earth at the enemy's approach so he should have no power over them; and has the elders, who once sat in the gate on thrones of judgment with their opinions treated as oracles, now sitting on the ground and dumb. Calvin will not let the verb behind purposed be weakened, since it would be flat to say God merely thought about destroying the wall when the word means resolved or decreed, and he sets that against the false imaginings by which men persuade themselves God is present in prosperity and absent in adversity; the wall did not fall by chance. He reads the sinking of the gates as their being fixed fast rather than fallen, so that they proved no hindrance at all, and derides a people who had thought their defences made the city impregnable; he takes being among the nations to mean there was no king at all. On the mourners he goes furthest, separating the signs from what they usually signify: sackcloth and dust were tokens of repentance, but here they are tokens of sorrow only, the elders having no resources and drawing the rest after them into an abject and fruitless lamentation with no regard to God in it, while hypocrites can put on sackcloth and make a show of repenting that is a false pretence.

Clarke and Wesley both take the measuring line for a line of devastation rather than a builder's, workmen using lines to mark what was to be cut down as well as raised. Clarke turns the sunken gates into a date, since sinking is what happens to gates long thrown down and neglected, so the captivity must already have lasted a considerable time, the king and princes being by then prisoners, unless the whole is spoken prophetically of what was still to come; and he makes an epigram of the elders' silence, that small griefs are eloquent and great ones dumb. Wesley puts the loss of the law as practice, no longer read, opened or observed, and notes how few prophets there were from that time until the gospel and how few even of those living had any revelation.

Henry strips the elders of their robes of state and puts them in the habit of mourners, seated as the friends of one afflicted man were seated with him, not opening their mouth in the gate, overwhelmed and not knowing what to say; and he refuses to sentimentalise the grief, quoting the Latin line that tears shed over lost property are genuine ones, since what these men had lost was their power and their wealth.

debates.question: Why are the gates said to be in the ground?

positions.position: They were broken down and buried under rubbish; the rabbinic story that they sank at the enemy's approach is a fable.
Buried under rubbish, and useless in any case since the bars are gone.
Sinking is what happens to gates long thrown down, so the detail dates the captivity as already of some length.
Fixed fast rather than fallen, so that they were no hindrance at all to the enemy.

debates.question: What do the sackcloth and dust of the elders signify?

positions.position: Tokens of sorrow only, not of repentance; the elders had no resources and led the rest into an abject lamentation with no regard to God.
Despondency in place of counsel: they sit as though the evil were inevitable.
Genuine mourning over real loss, though the loss mourned is power and wealth.
The silence of a grief too deep for speech.

outliers.claim: Takes the lamenting rampart literally enough to say that the very stones of the walls are imagined crying out and wailing over their own downfall.
Uses the sunken gates and the captive king as chronological evidence that the captivity had already lasted a considerable time when the poem was written, unless the whole is prophetic.

themes: The Lord hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together.
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the Lord.

The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, and keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.

11.pericope_label: Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city. They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers’ bosom. What thing shall I take to witness for thee? what thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee? Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch broaden the weeping beyond the prophet, holding he speaks not for himself only but in the name of all the godly; they report the poured-out liver as variously explained and refuse the reading that makes the liver the fountain of blood and so the seat of the animal life, denying that the proverb usually cited will bear it. On the question about a witness they treat the written form as a copyist's slip corrected in the margin, and take the verb in its favourable sense, to give testimony for instruction and comfort. Against the prophets they hold the false ones brought the calamity on by careless and foolish prophesying, promising peace where there was none, failing to expose the sin and guilt with a view to amendment, and never trying to restore the people to their right relation with the Lord or to avert the exile. Ellicott calls the poured-out liver unparalleled but easily explained, the liver being thought of with the heart and bowels as a seat of intense feeling, whether joy or sorrow, and here giving way without restraint — citing for that the same proverb his colleagues had refused. He thinks the cry for corn and wine paints what was passing before the writer's eye, though it may be the vivid present standing for the past; explains why the question about a witness has no answer, since a parallel that had been surmounted might have been cited in evidence and yielded some consolation, there being none, so that the ruin is illimitable as the ocean and past remedy; and notes the ironic use of the word for burdens, the thing such prophets delighted in.

Gill reports a Jewish commentator who put the weeping into the mouths of the elders just described, but takes it himself for the prophet's, who had wept his eyes dry, or rather blind, over calamities from which he personally gained liberty; he reads the question about a witness as a demand for argument and evidence, what could be produced to show any nation was ever in such a case; and he supplies specimens of the false prophecies, that the vessels would come back within two years and that the city would not be given up. Calvin makes the grief the point: in the deepest sorrow tears dry up at last, so a weeping that never ends is a sorrow which never ripens and must be very bitter, and the man who once asked who would turn his eyes into fountains now finds them consumed. With Gill he insists the cry for corn and wine is not the sucklings', since infants cannot ask and are not given wine, but children somewhat grown, the two being named together because one sort died in the streets and the other in the mother's bosom. He describes the convention of comfort being refused, since when we comfort a sick man we tell him he is neither the first nor the last and that the condition is common to mortals, whereas here such witnesses would avail nothing. On the prophets he turns the charge round on the hearers: the Jews had been inebriated with flatteries and destroyed themselves as though wilfully drinking sweet poison, sought to be deceived, cast themselves into the snare with avidity, and looked out flatterers for teachers.

Clarke draws the death of the children tightly, that in trying to draw nourishment from exhausted mothers they died in their bosoms, and asks how dreadfully afflicting it was; he prefers a rendering of the question about a witness that makes it what shall I urge to thee, and gives the breach as a flood of afflictions, a sea of troubles, an ocean of miseries. On the prophets he says they did not reprove for sin but flattered them in their transgressions, and instead of turning away the captivity by turning them from their sins pretended visions of good for them and false burdens for their enemies. Wesley is blunt that the prophet wept himself almost blind, solves the liver anatomically by putting the gall beneath it, treats the verse as one long expression of affliction, and makes the breach one in a sea wall, where the water comes with a torrent no defence can be made against.

debates.question: What does the poured-out liver mean?

positions.position: The liver as a seat of intense feeling alongside the heart and bowels, giving way without restraint.
Variously explained; the reading that makes it the fountain of blood and seat of animal life cannot be established from the proverb usually cited.
An anatomical detail, the gall lying beneath the liver, and the whole verse simply an expression of great affliction.

debates.question: Who is to blame for the false prophecies?

positions.position: The prophets, who promised peace, flattered the people in their transgressions and never exposed the guilt that might have averted the exile.
The people, who wilfully sought to be deceived, drank the flattery like sweet poison and looked out flatterers to be their teachers.

outliers.claim: Argues that a grief which never dries the eyes is worse than one that does, since in the deepest sorrow tears exhaust themselves at last, so an endless weeping is a sorrow that never ripens.
Notes the prophet's own position in the calamity he weeps over, since the fall of the city was what gained him his personal liberty.

themes: Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers’ bosom.

What thing shall I take to witness for thee? what thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee?
Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment.

15.pericope_label: All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth? All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed her up: certainly this is the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen it. The Lord hath done that which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old: he hath thrown down, and hath not pitied: and he hath caused thine enemy to rejoice over thee, he hath set up the horn of thine adversaries. Their heart cried unto the Lord, O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night: give thyself no rest; let not the apple of thine eye cease. Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the gestures: clapping here is not the sign of anger it can be elsewhere but of delight at another's injury, hissing and head-shaking are expressions of scorn, and the question about the perfection of beauty is scornful astonishment; in the enemies' own speech they note three verbs heaped without conjunctions, which suits an impassioned speaker, and that seeing there means living to see. They have God executing now what he threatened long ago and preparing the enemy's triumph himself, so that he alone can bring help, and will if he is entreated without ceasing; they rule the enemies out as the antecedent of the heart that cried, since the suffix cannot point back to them; and they read the summons about the night watches as at the head of each watch, so through the whole night. Ellicott says the enemies added bitterness by reminding Zion what she had been and setting it against what she was, describes their exultation as every feature of malignant hate, and finds an element of hope in the terrible thought that God is the author of the misery, since it is better to fall into the hands of God than of men and a suffering that comes as chastisement may be mitigated by repentance, the destroyer being also the healer. He treats the address to the wall as a deliberate boldness, the wall called on to take up its lamentation as though a human mourner and still the one addressed in the next verse, watching the children die and lifting her hands in supplication for them.

Gill separates the travellers who clap as they pass from the implacable enemies named next, and on the heart that cried reports a reading which makes it the enemies blaspheming, though he prefers the Jews, leaving it open that some cried sincerely and that all wished to be preserved; he also has it that God's doing, not the Chaldeans', was the true cause, whatever they ascribed to themselves. Calvin explains why the poet dwells so long on miseries everyone could see, namely that the Jews mourned without considering whence their evils came, and that suffering profits nobody who does not regard God's judgment in it. When enemies insult us, he says, we feel it, but grief soon blunts the feeling; the remedy is to stop fixing our thoughts on the insolence of men and remember that the wicked are the scourges by which God chastises. On the cry of the heart he denies any piety in it: there was no cry in their heart, and the phrase only measures how much grief there was, since silence is the token of patience while a man overcome forgets himself and bursts out; and this is a common cry which even the reprobate utter, nature teaching men to run to God under pressure, so that those with no fear of him still ask for mercy in extremity. He explains why fugitives already driven off like sheep should be told to arise: they were lying torpid in their sins, and it is that sloth the summons is aimed at.

Clarke doubts the title perfection of beauty ever fitted the city, which was never fine or splendid, and gives it to the Temple, the most splendid building in the world; he observes that the enemies had long envied Jerusalem and rejoiced when the day came. He interrupts with a textual observation of a different kind, that two of these verses stand out of the alphabet's order, the earlier opening with the letter that should follow and the later with the letter that should come first, so the pair ought to be interchanged. On the address to the wall he says plainly that he does not know what it means, that it is harsh to tell a wall to let tears run down day and night, that there is no parallel for it, and that one of his most ancient manuscripts simply omits the three words, leaving a text that runs smoothly without them; he takes the exhortation for the words of passers-by urging the people to plead, and pictures the watchmen sending up a prayer in place of calling the hour.

debates.question: Should the wall really be the one addressed?

positions.position: The sense is unknown and the words are harsh with no parallel; one ancient manuscript omits them and the text runs smoothly without.
The boldness is deliberate: the wall is called to lament as a human mourner and is still the one addressed in the next verse.

debates.question: Was the crying of the heart an act of piety?

positions.position: No; there was no cry in the heart, and it is the common cry even the reprobate utter under pressure, nature teaching men to call on a God they do not fear.
Perhaps in part; whether sincerely or not, some no doubt cried, and all wished to be preserved.
It is what seeing God's hand in the calamity drives the people to, and the summons that follows presses them to keep at it.

outliers.claim: Points out that two verses of this chapter stand out of alphabetical order and proposes interchanging them, the earlier carrying the letter that should come second and the later the letter that should come first.
Finds an element of hope in the very thought that God rather than the enemy is the author of the ruin, since a chastisement may be mitigated by repentance and the destroyer is also the healer.

All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed her up: certainly this is the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen it.

The Lord hath done that which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old: he hath thrown down, and hath not pitied: and he hath caused thine enemy to rejoice over thee, he hath set up the horn of thine adversaries.

20.pericope_label: Behold, O Lord, and consider to whom thou hast done this. Shall the women eat their fruit, and children of a span long? shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord? The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain them in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, and not pitied. Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the Lord’s anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the opening question to mean not what innocent and godly ones are being sacrificed, a reading they name and reject, but to what nation: not a heathen one but the people of God's own choosing, to whom all the promises had been given; the murder of priests and prophets in the sanctuary is what makes that the sense. They read the eating of children as inhuman conduct prompted by necessity, and judge that the imperfect verb in the last verse was chosen only to satisfy the alphabet, since the idea of custom or repetition does not suit, so the description simply continues. Ellicott agrees the question means the chosen people rather than a heathen nation, collects the parallels for the eating of children — that it was predicted, that it is the natural incident of a starving city, that it happened at another siege and would again under the Romans — lays the stress on the second horror, that the holiest place itself was profaned with the blood of God's priests and prophets, turns the mourner's thoughts from the massacre in the sanctuary to the slaughter done in every corner of the city, renders the last summons as for a solemn feast-day, and records a Greek rendering, followed by some, that turns the terrors round about into villages, which he dismisses.

Gill is careful that nothing is charged against God: the church neither accuses him of injustice nor complains of hard usage, but asks to be looked on with pity and leaves her case with him; the words, he notes, are supplied by the prophet as a prayer for others to use. He has young and old lying promiscuously in the public streets, fainting for want of food or killed outright, the enemy sparing neither age nor sex, and the terrors coming at God's call as soldiers at their general's, in such numbers as men once came from all Judea to one of the three yearly feasts. Calvin names and refuses the reading that makes the opening a comparison, whether any people was ever so severely afflicted, holding instead that the people set the covenant made with their fathers before God, as if to say that had he raged so against strangers there would be nothing to wonder at, but they are his heritage and peculiar people. He insists on the attribution in the following verse, that the text does not say they were slain by the enemy but by God, which was the hardest thing to get the Jews to accept, so filled were they with rage against the men who held the swords. On the last verse he adds the trumpets sounded when a feast was at hand, notes that the word for the assembly serves also for its place and time, agrees the alphabet required the future tense, observes that every version renders it as a past without saying why, and proposes reading it as a wish.

Clarke reads the opening question as a father asked whether he will destroy his own offspring, and puts the horror in the clause that follows, whether it was ever heard that a mother devoured her own child, a helpless infant of a span long; he grants such distress in a siege had been foretold in the law but thinks the fatherhood better supported by the context. On the last verse he has God calling terrors together to feast on the city as the people were once convoked from all parts to an annual festival, and supplies a parallel from a Roman poet on a civil war — nobility perishing with the common people, the sword ranging wide, blood standing in the temples and the stones slippery with slaughter, no man's age availing him — remarking that the lines read as if translated from these very verses. Wesley reads the summons the same way, that as the people were once called together from all parts on a solemn day, so now the terrible enemies are called together by God.

debates.question: What does the question to whom hast thou done this mean?

positions.position: To what nation: not a heathen one but the chosen people, which is why the murder of priests in the sanctuary is cited; the reading that asks what innocents are being sacrificed is rejected.
An appeal to the covenant, the people setting before God that they are his heritage and would not be a wonder if they were strangers; the reading that makes it a comparison of sufferings is refused.
An appeal to fatherhood: thou art our Father, we are thy children, wilt thou destroy thy own offspring.

debates.question: How should the verb in the closing summons be taken?

positions.position: As an imperfect chosen only to satisfy the alphabet, the description simply continuing, since custom or repetition does not suit.
The alphabet required the future, but every version renders it as a past without explanation; better read as a wish.

outliers.claim: Sets beside these verses a passage from a Roman poet on a civil war, blood standing in the temples and the stones slippery with slaughter, and remarks that the lines read as though they were a translation of the Hebrew.
Records and dismisses a Greek rendering, followed by some commentators, which turns the terrors round about into villages.

themes: Behold, O Lord, and consider to whom thou hast done this. Shall the women eat their fruit, and children of a span long? shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord?
The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain them in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, and not pitied.
Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the Lord’s anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.
